﻿function Get-MtAffectedObjectFromCache {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Derives the affected objects from the request caches in the current Maester session.

    .DESCRIPTION
    Walks $__MtSession.GraphCache and $__MtSession.GitHubCache — both keyed by request URL —
    and parses each key into a normalized object record (System / AnchorKind / Type / Id / SourceUri).

    Graph URIs yield:
    - Instance records when a path segment is a GUID (e.g. users/{id}/authentication/methods)
      or a quoted key (e.g. authenticationMethodConfigurations('Fido2'))
    - Singleton records for tenant-level config resources (e.g. policies/authorizationPolicy)
    - Collection records for plain collection reads (e.g. users, servicePrincipals)

    GitHub cache keys ({ApiVersion}|{AbsoluteUri}) yield External records for the
    organization or repository addressed by the request.

    This is a run-level view (what data the run touched), not per-test attribution.
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([object[]])]
    param()

    $guidPattern = '^[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-([0-9a-fA-F]{4}-){3}[0-9a-fA-F]{12}$'
    # Graph resources that are always tenant-level singletons when read without a key
    $singletonPrefixes = @(
        'policies', 'settings', 'organization', 'admin', 'identityProtection/settings',
        'reports', 'directory/recommendations', 'networkAccess'
    )
    # Graph collections whose keyed reads address a directory object the rest of the inventory
    # already knows under a canonical EntraID type. Mapping them here means a check that both
    # reads users/{id} and renders a portal link produces one object, not two.
    # applications is deliberately absent: the cache keys it by object id while the portal links
    # parsed from markdown carry the app id, so the two would not merge anyway.
    $directoryTypes = @{
        users             = 'User'
        groups            = 'Group'
        devices           = 'Device'
        servicePrincipals = 'ServicePrincipal'
        directoryRoles    = 'DirectoryRole'
    }

    # Keyed reads below these collections address an object the checks also link to under a
    # canonical type, so the read merges with it instead of listing it a second time as a Graph path:
    # accessPackages/{id}/accessPackageResourceRoleScopes is that access package.
    $keyedObjectTypes = @{
        'identityGovernance/entitlementManagement/accessPackages'        = 'AccessPackage'
        'identityGovernance/entitlementManagement/accessPackageCatalogs' = 'AccessPackageCatalog'
    }

    # Action endpoints are verbs, not resources: they address no object worth inventorying.
    $actionSegments = @('$batch', 'runHuntingQuery', 'getMemberGroups', 'getMemberObjects', 'checkMemberGroups')

    $records = [System.Collections.Generic.List[object]]::new()

    if ($__MtSession.GraphCache) {
        foreach ($key in $__MtSession.GraphCache.Keys) {
            # POST cache keys append "_<json body>" (or a bare "_" when the body is empty). A plain
            # underscore is part of the path: guest UPNs look like john_contoso.com#EXT#@tenant.
            $uri = ($key -split '_(?=[\{\[]|$)', 2)[0]
            if ($uri -notmatch '^https://[^/]*graph[^/]*/(v1\.0|beta)/(.+)$') { continue }
            $path = $Matches[2]
            # Strip query string
            $path = ($path -split '\?', 2)[0].TrimEnd('/')
            if ([string]::IsNullOrEmpty($path)) { continue }

            $segments = $path -split '/'
            if ($segments[-1] -in $actionSegments) { continue }

            # A keyed read of a directory collection is the object itself, whatever sub-resource
            # follows: users/{id}/authentication/methods is still that user, not a fifth object.
            # The key may be a GUID or a UPN, and a UPN must be recognised or it lands in Type,
            # where the report's PII redaction never reaches it.
            if ($segments.Count -ge 2 -and $directoryTypes.ContainsKey($segments[0])) {
                # Cache keys are AbsoluteUri values, so a UPN arrives percent-encoded (#EXT# as %23EXT%23).
                $directoryKey = [uri]::UnescapeDataString($segments[1])
            } else {
                $directoryKey = $null
            }

----
    Maester 2.x rows, and the severity is the one Defender for Identity reports for the issue.
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([pscustomobject])]
    param()

    try {
        $response = Invoke-MtGraphRequest -DisableCache -ApiVersion beta -RelativeUri 'security/identities/healthIssues' -OutputType Hashtable -ErrorAction Stop
    } catch {
        # Maester 2.x showed no rows here. Defender for Identity is not enabled, or the app lacks the permission.
        Add-MtTestResultDetail -SkippedBecause Custom -SkippedCustomReason "Microsoft Defender for Identity health issues could not be read. Defender for Identity may not be enabled in this tenant, or the SecurityIdentitiesHealth.Read.All permission is missing. Details: $($_.Exception.Message)"
    }
    $allHealthIssues = @($response.value | Where-Object { $_ })

    # Add domainNames and sensorDNSNames as string properties to identify unique health issues
    $allHealthIssues | ForEach-Object {
        $_ | Add-Member -NotePropertyName 'domainNamesString' -NotePropertyValue ($_.domainNames -join ',') -Force
        $_ | Add-Member -NotePropertyName 'sensorDNSNamesString' -NotePropertyValue ($_.sensorDNSNames -join ',') -Force
    }

    # Get unique health issues (duplicated entries will be created when status of an issue has been changed)
    $textInfo = (Get-Culture).TextInfo
    $healthIssues = [System.Collections.Generic.List[Object]]::new()
    $allHealthIssues | Group-Object -Property displayName, domainNamesString, sensorDNSNamesString | ForEach-Object {
        $uniqueHealthIssue = $_.Group | Sort-Object -Property createdDateTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 1
        $uniqueHealthIssue.severity = $textInfo.ToTitleCase($uniqueHealthIssue.severity) # We need title case to be compatible with Maester report
        $uniqueHealthIssue.status = $textInfo.ToTitleCase($uniqueHealthIssue.status) # It just looks better...
        $healthIssues.Add($uniqueHealthIssue) | Out-Null
    }

    # Group all latest issues based on displayName to group sensors based on particular issue

## Hard rules

- Generated content — regenerate, never hand-edit: `website/docs/commands/`,
  `website/docs/tests/`, `website/versioned_docs/`, everything under
  `powershell/internal/generated/`, and the native `tests/eidsca/Test.EIDSCA.*` and
  `tests/orca/Test.ORCA.*` files the generators in `build/eidsca/` and `build/orca/`
  write. Edit the PowerShell source, comment-based help or generator templates and let
  automation regenerate. `powershell/assets/ConsoleContributors.json` (the dashboard's
  Featured contributor list) is written by `./build/Update-ConsoleContributors.ps1` from
  the website's contributor data.
- A test is mapped to a framework in one place: the `Control` attribute, `<framework-key>:<requirement-id>`. A
  CIS test carries `Control = 'cis-m365:5.1.5.1'`, a CISA test `Control = 'cisa-scuba:MS.AAD.3.1'`, and any other
  test may name the same requirements. An ASD test carries `Control = 'essential-eight:ISM-1504'` (or `ism:<id>` for a
  control outside the maturity model). Every test in `tests/cis`, `tests/cisa` and `tests/asd` must name a requirement of its
  suite's framework. The engine builds `Benchmark` from the first `Control` that a framework file knows and adds
  that requirement's `Related` references to `Control`; do not repeat those, and do not add benchmark tags.
- A framework file is a catalogue, not a list of tests: `tests/<suite>/frameworks/<key>.json`
  (`tests/cis/frameworks/cis-m365.json`, `tests/cis/frameworks/cis-github.json`,
  `tests/cisa/frameworks/cisa-scuba.json`, and the generated `tests/asd/frameworks/essential-eight.json` and
  `tests/asd/frameworks/ism.json`, written by `build/asd/Update-AsdFramework.ps1` from the ISM OSCAL release),
  declared in the suite's `suite.json` (`Frameworks`: `Key`,
  `Version`). It holds the framework's name and version and each requirement's `Id` and facts (CIS `Level` and
  `Profile`; CISA `Criticality`, `Upstream` and `Related` NIST references; Essential Eight `Level` and `Strategy`;
  ISM `Guideline`, `Section` and `Applicability`), never the text of a benchmark and
  never a `Tests` list. When a new test implements a requirement the file does not have, add the requirement in
  the same commit, or `./build/Build-MaesterModule.ps1` and the unit tests fail.

content.text:
The #2625 description now covers the new commit. The #2620 tests are still running; when they finish I'll push its tabs fix, then run the #2619 tests on its 2.1.12/2.1.13 change.

**Is the CodeRabbit comment in your screenshot a risk?** Not today. Unlike the earlier comments, it doesn't ask us to turn caching off. It says the cache key ignores `-OutputType`, which is true. But only MT.1024 and MT.1059 ask for `Hashtable` output, and no other code reads either of their URLs. So no other caller can get a cached copy in the wrong form. It would only bite if a later check or custom test read one of those two URLs in the default form.

**How CodeRabbit is told to stop.** I pushed `d297c93` to #2625 with two changes:
- **`.coderabbit.yaml`:** a new instruction for `powershell/`, `tests/` and `packs/`. It tells CodeRabbit that checks read through the session cache by design. It must never suggest `-DisableCache` or getting around the cache, not even to pick up changes made during a run. It also names the unit test that would fail. Suggestions about how the cache itself works stay allowed, so a comment like this one about the cache key can still come through.
- **`AGENTS.md`:** the same rule under Hard rules. CodeRabbit also reads `AGENTS.md` as coding guidance, and so do other agents and contributors.

Both take effect once #2625 merges, because CodeRabbit reads its settings from main.

content.text:
Review target: `2625`

`high effort → 8 inline angles → dedup (no verify) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle + 1 conventions angle, up to 6 each)

Run **8 independent finder angles** in sequence yourself, in THIS context — do NOT spawn subagents for them. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

### Conventions (CLAUDE.md)

Find the CLAUDE.md files that govern the changed code: the user-level
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the repo-root CLAUDE.md, plus any CLAUDE.md or
CLAUDE.local.md in a directory that is an ancestor of a changed file (a
directory's CLAUDE.md only applies to files at or below it). Read each one
that exists, then check the diff for clear violations of the rules they state.

Only flag a violation when you can quote the exact rule and the exact line
that breaks it — no style preferences, no vague "spirit of the doc"
inferences. In the finding, name the CLAUDE.md path and quote the rule so the
report can cite it. If no CLAUDE.md applies, return nothing for this angle.

Cleanup, altitude, and conventions candidates use the same
`file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in `failure_scenario`, state the concrete
cost (what is duplicated, wasted, harder to maintain, or which CLAUDE.md rule
is broken) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank cleanup,
altitude, and conventions findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates are the dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Dedup only (no verify)

Pool all candidates. Dedup near-duplicates only (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). Do NOT run verifiers; do NOT re-judge. Sort by severity.

## Output

Target **at least 5 findings**. If fewer genuine findings exist, emit what you have — do not invent to hit the floor.

Call the ReportFindings tool once to report this review's results
with `{level, findings}`. `findings` is at most 10 entries ranked
most-severe first; each entry has `file`, `line`, `summary`,
`short_summary` — the claim compressed to ≤60 characters, no rationale
or consequence clause — `failure_scenario`, and `category` — a short kebab-case slug for the angle
that produced it (`correctness`, `simplification`, `efficiency`,
`reuse`, `altitude`, `conventions`, or a more specific slug like
`test-coverage` when one fits better) — plus `verdict` when a verify pass
produced one. If more than 10 survive, keep the 10 most severe. If
nothing survives, call it with an empty array. Do not also print
the findings as text, and do not create or publish an artifact of the review -
the tool call is the report.


## If findings are fixed later

Whenever reported findings get fixed later in this session - the user asks you
to fix them, or later work fixes them incidentally - you MUST call ReportFindings again with the same findings, each
carrying an `outcome`: `fixed`, `no_change_needed` (the finding was wrong or
already handled), or `skipped` (real but not applied). Do not repeat the
findings as text.
Make that call immediately after the fixes land, before any prose summary; the
host UI's per-finding status updates only from it, and without it the findings
stay marked unresolved.

+function Test-MtGraphNotFoundError {
+    <#
+    .SYNOPSIS
+    Internal: Returns whether a Microsoft Graph ErrorRecord is a 404 Not Found.
+
+    .DESCRIPTION
+    Checks the response status code in its enum, string and integer forms, then the exception's own StatusCode
+    property, then the message, because the form depends on the Graph SDK and PowerShell version.
+    #>
+    [CmdletBinding()]
+    [OutputType([bool])]
+    param(
+        # The ErrorRecord caught from a Graph request.
+        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
+        [System.Management.Automation.ErrorRecord]$ErrorRecord
+    )
+
+    $responseStatusCode = $ErrorRecord.Exception.Response.StatusCode
+    $exceptionStatusCode = $ErrorRecord.Exception.StatusCode
+    return ($responseStatusCode -eq [System.Net.HttpStatusCode]::NotFound) -or
+        ($responseStatusCode -eq 'NotFound') -or
+        ($responseStatusCode -eq 404) -or
+        ($exceptionStatusCode -eq [System.Net.HttpStatusCode]::NotFound) -or
+        ($ErrorRecord.Exception.Message -match 'NotFound|404')
+}

findings.short_summary: Message regex 'NotFound|404' can misclassify errors
findings.summary: The fallback `$ErrorRecord.Exception.Message -match 'NotFound|404'` is unanchored, so any message containing "404" (an object id, a Retry-After value, a URL) is treated as not found and silently skipped.
findings.failure_scenario: A 403 or 429 whose message includes a group id like `...4048-...` or `retry after 404 ms` matches the regex. `Get-MtGroupMember` returns $null, and the check passes without the group's members: the false pass this PR is meant to remove.

findings.short_summary: String throw discards the original ErrorRecord/status
findings.summary: `throw "Could not read group ...: $($_.Exception.Message)"` replaces the HttpResponseException with a plain RuntimeException, so callers lose the status code and the inner exception.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller or the engine that wants to treat 429/throttling differently from 403, or log the Graph request id, gets only a string. `Test-MtGraphNotFoundError` on the rethrown error from a nested group can only match the message text, which compounds the regex problem above.

findings.short_summary: Hashtable responses now cached under a type-blind key
findings.summary: Removing -DisableCache means MT.1024 and MT.1059 now store `-OutputType Hashtable` responses in the Graph cache, whose key ignores OutputType (the CodeRabbit finding).
findings.failure_scenario: A custom test or pack reads `directory/recommendations?$expand=impactedResources` or `security/identities/healthIssues` with the default PSObject output after MT.1024 or MT.1059 has run, and gets the cached Hashtable. findings.short_summary: MT.1059 mutates the now-cached response objects

findings.failure_scenario: Any later reader of `security/identities/healthIssues` in the same session, such as a family instance, a custom test or the affected-objects report, sees the title-cased severity and the injected `domainNamesString`/`sensorDNSNamesString` properties instead of Graph's data.

---
name: maester-pr-desk
description: Merill's PR review desk for maester365/maester. Use when he asks to "review the new PRs", "update the PR desk", "check which PRs can merge", or "process the PR desk" (act on what he queued). Reviews open PRs, writes a verdict, findings, maintainer fixes and a draft comment for each into the PR Desk artifact, then, once he queues decisions there, posts the reviews, pushes the fixes and merges.
---

# Maester PR Desk

The desk is a published artifact with a small database:
**https://claude.ai/artifact/UohxsGPhGM6VveP4w7ayvo**

The page source is `pr-desk.html`, in this folder. To change the page, edit that file and publish it with the Artifact tool and that `url`; read the artifact first in a new conversation. Read and write its data with the `ArtifactData` tool, using the same `url`.

There are two modes. Merill says which one he wants.

## Mode 1: review ("review the new PRs", "update the desk")

1. **List.** Run `gh pr list --state open` for maester365/maester. Skip drafts; at most, mention them in one line.
   - `ArtifactData list prs` shows what is already on the desk.
   - Review a PR again only if it is new, or its head SHA differs from `prs/<n>.headSha`.
   - If a PR has merged or closed, set `verdict` to `merged` or `closed` and keep its doc as history.
2. **Review.** Fetch each PR's head as `refs/remotes/pr/<n>`: `git fetch origin pull/<n>/head:refs/remotes/pr/<n>`. Never check out over Merill's working branch.
   - Read the existing review threads first, so you don't repeat points that are resolved.
   - Do small PRs inline. Send larger ones to `maester-test-expert` subagents in parallel, read-only.
   - Ask each subagent for: a verdict, the CI cause and fix, behaviour changes against main, findings with file:line, a draft comment, and fixes a maintainer could make.
   - Apply AGENTS.md: the attribute rubric, repository layout, generated files, and benchmark shims. Also check for changes to exported public commands.
   - **Verify the one or two claims that matter** before they go into a comment. For example, read the diff for a "breaking change", or look up Graph permissions with the `msgraph` skill. Don't relay subagent claims unchecked.
   - Check whether CI failures are the PR's fault or come from main. A stale generated file on main is a common cause: `test-builder.json`, `selection.json`, or a broken docs link.
3. **Write** one `prs/<number>` doc per PR, all in a single `ArtifactData batch`, using the schema below.
4. **Report** in chat: a short line per PR, and the desk link. Don't post anything to GitHub in this mode.

## Mode 2: act ("process the PR desk")

1. Run `ArtifactData list decisions` and pick the docs where `status == "queued"`. Ignore `draft` and `hold`.
2. For each one, before acting:
   - If `decision.prSha` or `prs.headSha` differs from the PR's current head on GitHub, stop for that PR. Re-review it, update its doc, set the decision back to `draft` with a note in `prs.outcome`, and tell Merill.
   - Make sure the comment still matches the fixes he ticked. If it still asks the author for a ticked fix (the fix's `ask` phrase), or says "I pushed" for a fix he left unticked, stop and ask him rather than editing his text.
3. **Fixes:** apply each ticked `fixes[].id` on the contributor's branch.
   - Use a worktree under the scratchpad, never the main checkout. The PR must have `maintainerCanModify` set.
   - Prefer merging main to rebasing, so you never force-push over a contributor's history.
   - Regenerate generated files with their build scripts, and run `./powershell/tests/pester.ps1` before pushing.
   - The commit message ends with the session's Co-Authored-By line.
   - A fix that targets main, like `builder-main`, becomes its own branch and PR off main.
4. **Review:** `event` APPROVE, REQUEST_CHANGES or COMMENT → `gh pr review <n> --approve|--request-changes|--comment --body-file <file>`. `NONE` → post nothing.
   - The comment is Merill's text, edited on the desk. Post it word for word, then add the block the page shows under "Added below your comment": a blank line, `**Changes I pushed to your branch:**`, then `- <note>` for each ticked fix that isn't `internal`, in `fixes[]` order. Leave the block out if a fix wasn't pushed, and say so in `outcome`.
   - Do the steps in the order the card's "Claude will" box lists them: internal fixes, then the branch fixes, then the review, then the merge.
   - **Assignee:** when the PR now waits on its author (REQUEST_CHANGES, or a NONE/COMMENT on a PR whose changes are still requested), assign the author: `gh pr edit <n> --add-assignee <author>`. When you approve or merge, remove the author if they are assigned: `--remove-assignee <author>`.
5. **Merge:** only if `merge` is true and CI is green on the commit you just pushed. Use `gh pr merge <n> --merge`.
   - Never enable auto-merge. If CI is still running, leave the PR and say so.
6. **Record:** update `decisions/<n>` to `status: "done"` with `doneAt`, and `prs/<n>.outcome` with one line on what happened, including links or SHAs.
   - Pin each write to the version you read, with `if_version`.
7. **Report** in chat what was posted, pushed and merged, and anything you skipped and why.

## Data schema

`prs/<number>` is written by Claude:
- **Identity:** `number`, `title`, `author`, `url`, `headSha` (12 chars), `size` (`"+a/-d · n files"`).
- **State:** `merge` (`mergeable|conflicting|behind|blocked`), `ci` (`passing|failing|pending`), `ciNote`.
- **Verdict:** `verdict` (`ready|small-fix|changes|decision|merged|closed`), `order` (rank: ready first, then by complexity).
- **Review:** `reviewedAt` (ISO), `summary`, and `question`, used only when Merill must rule on something.
- **Findings:** `findings[]`, each `{sev: high|medium|low|nit, text, where}`.
- **Fixes:** `fixes[]`, each `{id, text, note, ask, internal, preselect}`. These are things we could do ourselves.
  - `text`: what we'll do, shown beside the checkbox.
  - `note`: the line added to the comment when it's ticked, in the past tense ("Added the missing trailing newline to `x.md`.").
  - `ask`: an exact phrase from the draft comment that asks the author for the same change. The page warns when the fix is ticked and the phrase is still in the comment.
  - `internal: true` for work that isn't on the author's branch (approving fork workflows, merging main before merge). It gets no `note` and isn't mentioned in the comment.
  - Write the draft comment so it reads right with the fixes unticked. The page adds the ticked fixes' notes.
- **Draft:** `event` (`APPROVE|REQUEST_CHANGES|COMMENT|NONE`) and `comment`, which is markdown for GitHub.
- **History:** `outcome`, a one-line log of the last action.

`decisions/<number>` is written by the page:
- **Review:** `comment`, `event`, `fixes[]` (ticked ids), `merge` (bool).
- **State:** `status` (`draft|queued|hold|done`), `prSha`, `decidedAt`, and `doneAt`, which Claude sets.

Inline text renders `` `code` `` and `**bold**`.

## Writing the comment

- Address the author with their real @login, and thank them once.
- Plain English, short bullets, and bold labels for the blocking items. No emoji, and no headings beyond bold.
- Say clearly what blocks the merge and what is optional.
- When CI fails because of main, tell them it isn't their fault and that we'll fix it.
- Never write "I pushed …" in the comment. The page adds pushed fixes from their `note`, so the comment matches what is ticked.

## Process notes

Merill's rulings go here as they come up.

- Skip contributors' draft PRs.
- Read the existing reviews before reviewing.
- A benchmark test that duplicates another suite's check is a shim.
- No "(Preview)" in test titles.
- Take `headSha` from `git rev-parse --short=12` or `gh`, never typed from memory. A wrong SHA looks like a moved PR.
- A PR that merged after he queued it can't be approved. Post the comment with `gh pr comment` and record that.
- Locally, `ZeroTrustAssessmentPack.Tests.ps1` "skips the family when the module is not installed" fails because the module is installed on his Mac. Ignore it; every other failure blocks a push.
- Write large desk docs from a JSON file (`ArtifactData set` with `file_path`); long inline JSON can fail to parse.
- A contributor who pushes a change and then reverts it may reopen it as a new PR. Compare the two with `git patch-id`.
- Pushing to a contributor's branch dismisses the approvals already on the PR. Re-approve after the push, not before.
- Fork workflows can wait at `action_required` after we push. Approving them is an `internal` fix.
- When a PR moves after a decision was `done`, set its decision back to `draft` with the new draft, so it shows under Needs you.
- A PR waiting on its author is assigned to them, so the GitHub list shows whose move it is (ruling 2026-10-31).
- CIS checks follow the benchmark's PowerShell audit procedure in scope, values and missing data (ruling 2026-10-31; written up in the repo's maester-test-expert skill and writing-tests guide, "What a benchmark test evaluates"). Before asking an author to widen or narrow a CIS check, read the audit section in `~/Downloads/REDACTED.0.0.pdf` (`pdftotext -layout`) and quote it. Example: 6.2.1 checks every outbound policy; 2.1.15 checks only Default.
- When a fix is small and the PR allows maintainer edits, make it ourselves rather than asking the author.

content.text:
I've made the #2619 and #2620 fixes myself, and their cards now hold approval drafts for you to queue. The CIS rule is in its own PR. CI is still running on both contributor branches.

**#2620:** I pushed `d568f1e` to the author's branch, replacing the tabs in the 6.1.2 script with spaces.
- **Tests:** they passed, apart from the ZeroTrustAssessment test that always fails on your Mac. One more failure was the stale `test-builder.json` from before #2622; the branch hasn't picked up that fix from main yet.
- **Draft approval:** keeps the stricter 6.2.1, because the CIS audit checks every outbound policy. It also thanks the author for the remediation and for listing the behaviour changes, and points to #2626.

**#2619:** I pushed `cc89d3f`, so 2.1.12 and 2.1.13 now fail with "compliance could not be established" when no Default connection filter policy comes back, instead of passing.
- **Tests:** only the ZeroTrustAssessment failure.
- **Draft approval:** under the new rule, most of our earlier review falls away, and the draft says so point by point:
  - **2.1.15:** the audit reads Default only, so the author's change is right.
  - **2.1.6:** following custom policies matches the audit's note about the highest-priority policy.
  - **2.1.11:** the 90% threshold comes from the CIS audit script, and rules were already matched on Id, Name and Identity.
  - **2.1.7:** the audit reads only `AntiPhishRule`, so our preset point doesn't apply.
  - **2.1.4 and 2.1.7 scope:** the audit asks for a judgement call here.
- **Still to clear:** our earlier request for changes on #2619 stays in place until you queue the approval.

**[#2626](https://github.com/maester365/maester/pull/2626), the CIS rule:** a CIS test does what the benchmark's PowerShell audit does, in three ways:
- **Scope:** it reads the same objects.
- **Values:** it uses the same thresholds.
- **Missing data:** it fails or errors when the audited object is missing, and never passes.

The rule is now in:
- the writing-tests guide, as "What a benchmark test evaluates";
- the test-expert skill, including its review checklist;
- `.coderabbit.yaml`, for `tests/cis` and `tests/cisa`.

#2625 and #2626 both edit the same spot in `.coderabbit.yaml`, so whichever merges second will need that one-line conflict fixed.

**PR Desk skill:** it now records three rulings:
- the CIS audit rule, with the PDF to read;
- make small fixes ourselves when the PR allows it;
- describe fixes we've already pushed in the comment, rather than listing them as fixes to tick.

fix: tighten group read errors, key the cache by output type, widen the cache guard

- Test-MtGraphNotFoundError reads the status code from the exception and its
  inner exception, and only falls back to the Graph error code or a "Not Found"
  status in the message. A bare "404" in a message no longer counts, so an
  object id or Retry-After value can't turn a 403 into a skipped group.
- Get-MtGroupMember reads groups/{id}/members directly (one request instead of
  two) and throws an ErrorRecord that keeps the Graph exception as its inner
  exception. It uses throw rather than ThrowTerminatingError so the calling
  check stops.
- Invoke-MtGraphRequest adds "_[<OutputType>]" to the cache key for non-default
  output types, so a Hashtable response is never served to a PSObject caller.
  The affected-object inventory already strips "_[" suffixes.
- MT.1059 works on copies of the cached response instead of changing it.
- GraphCacheUsage.Tests.ps1 also fails on NoCache, ClearCache, Clear-Mt*Cache
  calls, -DisableCache:$true, and checks that reset $__MtSession caches.
- Get-MtRoleMember help says results come from the session cache.
- Rename the test helper New-HttpError to Get-HttpError (PSScriptAnalyzer
  PSUseShouldProcessForStateChangingFunctions).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git push -q origin HEAD:fix/graph-cache-in-checks 2>&1 | grep -v "^remote"; git log -1 --format=%h

** Minor** · **Functional Correctness** · **Quick win**

**Tighten the message fallback. It can classify a non-404 error as not found.**

`-match 'NotFound|404'` is an unanchored substring match. Graph error messages often contain GUIDs such as request IDs, client request IDs and resource IDs. About 1 in 4,000 positions in a hex GUID starts the substring `404`, so a given GUID has a small but real chance of containing it. A 403 or 429 error whose message contains such a GUID returns `$true`. `Get-MtGroupMember` then skips the group and returns `$null`. A check can pass without reading the members. This is the outcome the PR is meant to prevent.

**Review fixes:**
- **404 check:** `Test-MtGraphNotFoundError` now reads the status code from the error and the error wrapped inside it. It only falls back to the message for `Request_ResourceNotFound` or a "Not Found" status. A stray "404" inside an object id or retry delay no longer counts, which I checked against six sample errors.
- **Error kept:** `Get-MtGroupMember` throws an error that keeps the Graph exception inside, so its status code can still be read.
  - It uses `throw`, not `$PSCmdlet.ThrowTerminatingError`. The second only stops the caller's current line, so `Get-MtRoleMember` would have carried on with no members, which is the same false pass we're removing.
  - A new test checks that the calling script stops.
- **One request per group:** `Get-MtGroupMember` no longer reads the group itself before its members.
- **Cache key:** a `Hashtable` response is now cached under its own key (`…_[Hashtable]`), so a default caller never gets one. The affected-objects report already strips that suffix, and a test confirms it.

# AGENTS.md

Maester is a PowerShell framework for monitoring Microsoft 365 security
configuration, with its own test engine. Pester is used only for the module's unit tests
and to run users' Pester-format custom tests. Requires PowerShell 7.4+. Monorepo: `powershell/` (module source),
`tests/` (security checks shipped to users), `src/Maester.Engine/` (C# engine core,
built DLL committed in `powershell/lib/`), `build/`, `website/` (Docusaurus,
maester.dev), `report/` (React app that builds the HTML report template).

## Two unrelated test trees — don't mix them

- `tests/` — Maester **security checks** that ship to end-user tenants, run via
  `Invoke-Maester`. Each check is a native test: `tests/<suite>/[<service>/]Test.<ID>.ps1`
  (one function with a `[MaesterTest(...)]` attribute) plus `Test.<ID>.md`. No
  `*.Tests.ps1` wrappers, no connection/licence guards, no outer try/catch: declare
  `Service`/`License` and the engine handles them. Scaffold with `New-MtTest`,
  validate with `Get-MtTest <ID>` (`Get-MtTest -Path` applies the rules of a custom test
  and does not report a missing attribute), run with `Invoke-MtTest -Path`; `Convert-MtTest`
  converts users' Pester-format tests. New MT.xxxx checks go here; follow
  `.github/skills/maester-test-expert/SKILL.md` and `website/docs/writing-tests/index.mdx`,
  and choose the attribute values with `website/docs/writing-tests/attribute-rubric.md`
  (see "Reviewing a test's attributes" below).
- `powershell/tests/` — **unit tests for the module itself**.

## Commands

- Unit tests: `./powershell/tests/pester.ps1` — run before pushing. These enforce
  naming, exports, help, and PSScriptAnalyzer conventions; fix what they flag.
- Build module: `./build/Build-MaesterModule.ps1`; validate: `./build/Test-MaesterModuleOutput.ps1`
- Website: `cd website && npm ci && npm start` · Report: `cd report && npm ci && npm run build`

## Hard rules

- Generated content — regenerate, never hand-edit: `website/docs/commands/`,
  `website/docs/tests/`, `website/versioned_docs/`, everything under
  `powershell/internal/generated/`, and the native `tests/eidsca/Test.EIDSCA.*` and
  `tests/orca/Test.ORCA.*` files the generators in `build/eidsca/` and `build/orca/`
  write. Edit the PowerShell source, comment-based help or generator templates and let
  automation regenerate. `powershell/assets/ConsoleContributors.json` (the dashboard's
  Featured contributor list) is written by `./build/Update-ConsoleContributors.ps1` from
  the website's contributor data.
- A test is mapped to a framework in one place: the `Control` attribute, `<framework-key>:<requirement-id>`. A
  CIS test carries `Control = 'cis-m365:5.1.5.1'`, a CISA test `Control = 'cisa-scuba:MS.AAD.3.1'`, and any other
  test may name the same requirements. Every test in `tests/cis` and `tests/cisa` must name a requirement of its
  suite's framework. The engine builds `Benchmark` from the first `Control` that a framework file knows and adds
  that requirement's `Related` references to `Control`; do not repeat those, and do not add benchmark tags.
- A framework file is a catalogue, not a list of tests: `tests/<suite>/frameworks/<key>.json`
  (`tests/cis/frameworks/cis-m365.json`, `tests/cis/frameworks/cis-github.json`,
  `tests/cisa/frameworks/cisa-scuba.json`), declared in the suite's `suite.json` (`Frameworks`: `Key`,
  `Version`). It holds the framework's name and version and each requirement's `Id` and facts (CIS `Level` and
  `Profile`; CISA `Criticality`, `Upstream` and `Related` NIST references), never the text of a benchmark and
  never a `Tests` list. When a new test implements a requirement the file does not have, add the requirement in
  the same commit, or `./build/Build-MaesterModule.ps1` and the unit tests fail.

## Repository layout — where files go

Full rules and reasoning: `website/docs/contributing.md` ("Repository layout"), published at
https://maester.dev/docs/next/contributing#repository-layout. `powershell/tests/general/RepositoryLayout.Tests.ps1`
enforces them. When writing or reviewing a change, check every added, moved or renamed file:

- Folder names under `tests/`, `powershell/` and `build/` are lowercase kebab-case
  (`global-secure-access`, not `GlobalSecureAccess`). No two paths may differ only in case.
- One name per service, the same everywhere: `ad`, `azure`, `azure-devops`, `copilot`,
  `copilot-studio`, `defender`, `entra`, `exchange`, `foundry`, `github`,
  `global-secure-access`, `graph`, `intune`, `purview`, `sharepoint`, `teams`, `xspm`.
  Folders name the product whose settings a check reads, never a theme: an AI check goes in
  the folder of its product (an Entra agent identity check in `entra/`) and declares
  `Area = 'ai'`. A new service must be added to the guide and the test.
- `tests/<suite>/` holds only `Test.<ID>.ps1`, `Test.<ID>.md`, `suite.json` and `README.md`, plus the suite's
  framework files, `frameworks/<key>.json` beside its `suite.json` (lowercase key; nothing else goes in a
  `frameworks/` folder).
  Suites: `maester/<service>/` (plus `drift/`; `maester/xspm/` has its own suite.json),
  `cis/`, `cisa/<service>/`, `ad/<area>/`, generated `eidsca/` and `orca/`, and `custom/`
  (reserved for users; never commit tests there).
- `powershell/public/` (exported) is grouped by job: `run/`, `connect/`, `report/`, `app/`,
  `packs/`, `services/<service>/`. `powershell/internal/` uses `engine/`, `session/`, `connect/`,
  `report/`, `app/`, `packs/`, `services/<service>/`, `checks/<suite>/<service>/`, `generated/`,
  `utility/`. Nothing sits directly in `public/` or `internal/`.
- `packs/<name>/` at the repository root holds the Maester Packs that ship with Maester (ID `maester.<name>`,
  a code of the pack's own such as `ZTA`, test IDs `<Code>.<n>` without the `MP.` that installed packs use). They are not under `tests/`: a pack loads into its own private
  module, and its rows carry `Source = Custom` and `Package`. See `packs/README.md`.
- Put a function by its job, not by the check that first needed it: reusable data access
  for a service goes in `internal/services/<service>/`; logic only one suite's checks use
  goes in `internal/checks/<suite>/<service>/`; a helper users call from custom tests goes
  in `public/services/<service>/` (and in the manifest's `FunctionsToExport`).
- One function per file, named `Verb-Noun.ps1` after the function, with an approved verb.
- Custom tests can call only exported commands. To make an internal helper available to them,
  `git mv` it from `internal/services/<service>/` to `public/services/<service>/`, add it to
  `FunctionsToExport`, and give it full comment-based help (see "Making an internal helper public"
  in the contributing guide). Exporting a command makes it public API; flag a promotion in review.

## Reviewing a test's attributes

Every built-in test declares what it is about, how urgent a failure is and which attack techniques
it addresses: `Product`, `Feature`, `Area`, `ResourceType`, `Severity`, `UserImpact`,
`ImplementationCost`, `Mitre` and, where one applies, `RelatedProduct`. The rules for each value
are in `website/docs/writing-tests/attribute-rubric.md` (the rubric); the allowed keys are in
`powershell/assets/MaesterTaxonomy.psd1`.

When you write, change or review a test, check its attributes against the rubric as a separate
step, after the code review and before you approve or hand off:

1. Read the test's `.ps1` and `.md` and state in one sentence what it checks and what the fix is.
2. For each attribute that is new or changed, decide whether the declared value fits the rubric. A
   value fails only when the rubric clearly gives a different one; say which value and which rule.
3. Fail the review if any value does not fit. Do not approve with a note to fix it later.

Three things enforce this, in order:

- `powershell/tests/general/NativeTestAttributes.Tests.ps1` fails on anything mechanical: a missing
  attribute, a key that is not in the taxonomy, a retired ATT&CK technique, a taxonomy tag on a
  built-in test.
- The `attribute-review` workflow (`.github/workflows/attribute-review.yaml`) runs a reviewer model
  against the rubric on every pull request that adds a test or changes one of these attributes, and
  fails the check with the value it expected and the reason. It calls the Claude API with the
  `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` secret; without the secret it reports that the review was skipped. To run
  the same review locally before pushing, set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and run
  `./build/review/Invoke-MtAttributeReview.ps1 -BaseRef origin/main -OutputPath ./TestResults`
  (`TestResults/` is ignored by git; without `-OutputPath` the report is written to the current
  folder).
- The person or agent reviewing the pull request applies the same rubric and is the last word. A
  maintainer who disagrees with the workflow can apply the `attribute-review-override` label and
  should say why in the pull request.

## Labelling pull requests, issues and discussions

Labels follow one rubric so the queue can be filtered by status, type and product. The
labels are defined in `.github/labels.json`; the rules for choosing them are in
`.github/skills/maester-triage/SKILL.md`. To triage, use the `maester-triage` agent (or follow
the skill directly): it shows its plan before changing anything and only ever changes labels.
After editing `.github/labels.json`, run `./build/github/Sync-GitHubLabels.ps1` to see the
changes and `-Apply` to make them. `-Apply` creates, renames and updates labels and copies a merged
label onto the items that carry the old one; add `-DeleteMerged` to also delete the old labels.

## Agents and skills

The agents and skills in this repository are listed in `website/docs/agents-and-skills.md`. Each
has one source file: `.github/agents/<name>.agent.md` or `.github/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. The
Claude Code copies under `.claude/agents/` and `.claude/skills/`, and that docs page, are generated
from them by `./build/github/Update-AgentFiles.ps1`. Edit the source file, run the script, and
commit both; never edit a generated copy. `powershell/tests/general/AgentFiles.Tests.ps1` fails
when they drift.

- [Contributors attribution system](contributors-attribution-system.md) — registry + git-derived credits for maester.dev
- [Maester 3.0 design](maester-3-design.md) — design doc, owner rulings, status (M0–M9 done on PR 2334, design changes awaiting sign-off)
- [Maester Packs design](maester-marketplace-design.md) — packs/connectors marketplace draft + mockup; owner rulings 2026-10-07, some items open
- [Maester 3.0 console output](maester-3-console-output.md) — TUI/perf rulings 2026-10-10, shipped on PR 2334, open follow-ups; 2026-10-18 boxed main column + pipeline built (uncommitted branch)
- [Test taxonomy research](maester-test-taxonomy-research.md) — framework/MITRE mapping research + clean-slate attribute design; lives in maester-cloud, never in Maester; Category/Tag may change
- [Console easter egg](maester-console-easter-egg.md) — hidden game in the 3.0 dashboard; stealth rule (no docs, no push until asked), trigger `dead`
- [Preview test titles](preview-test-titles.md) — no "(Preview)" in titles; read existing PR reviews before reviewing
- [Skip draft PRs](skip-draft-prs.md) — ignore contributors' draft PRs when triaging; one-line mention at most
- [Benchmark shims](map-benchmarks-to-existing-tests.md) — a benchmark test duplicating another suite's check is a shim; review new tests for duplicates against the benchmark's own sources
- [PR Desk workflow](maester-pr-desk.md) — PR reviews go through the PR Desk artifact + ~/.claude/skills/maester-pr-desk skill

---
name: maester-pr-desk
description: Merill's PR review desk for maester365/maester. Use when he asks to "review the new PRs", "update the PR desk", "check which PRs can merge", or "process the PR desk" (act on what he queued). Reviews open PRs, writes a verdict, findings, maintainer fixes and a draft comment for each into the PR Desk artifact, then, once he queues decisions there, posts the reviews, pushes the fixes and merges.
---

# Maester PR Desk

The desk is a published artifact with a small database:
**https://claude.ai/artifact/UohxsGPhGM6VveP4w7ayvo**

The page source is `pr-desk.html`, in this folder. To change the page, edit that file and publish it with the Artifact tool and that `url`; read the artifact first in a new conversation. Read and write its data with the `ArtifactData` tool, using the same `url`.

There are two modes. Merill says which one he wants.

## Mode 1: review ("review the new PRs", "update the desk")

1. **List.** Run `gh pr list --state open` for maester365/maester. Skip drafts; at most, mention them in one line.
   - `ArtifactData list prs` shows what is already on the desk.
   - Review a PR again only if it is new, or its head SHA differs from `prs/<n>.headSha`.
   - If a PR has merged or closed, set `verdict` to `merged` or `closed` and keep its doc as history.
2. **Review.** Fetch each PR's head as `refs/remotes/pr/<n>`: `git fetch origin pull/<n>/head:refs/remotes/pr/<n>`. Never check out over Merill's working branch.
   - Read the existing review threads first, so you don't repeat points that are resolved.
   - Do small PRs inline. Send larger ones to `maester-test-expert` subagents in parallel, read-only.
   - Ask each subagent for: a verdict, the CI cause and fix, behaviour changes against main, findings with file:line, a draft comment, and fixes a maintainer could make.
   - Apply AGENTS.md: the attribute rubric, repository layout, generated files, and benchmark shims. Also check for changes to exported public commands.
   - **Verify the one or two claims that matter** before they go into a comment. For example, read the diff for a "breaking change", or look up Graph permissions with the `msgraph` skill. Don't relay subagent claims unchecked.
   - Check whether CI failures are the PR's fault or come from main. A stale generated file on main is a common cause: `test-builder.json`, `selection.json`, or a broken docs link.
3. **Write** one `prs/<number>` doc per PR, all in a single `ArtifactData batch`, using the schema below.
4. **Report** in chat: a short line per PR, and the desk link. Don't post anything to GitHub in this mode.

## Mode 2: act ("process the PR desk")

1. Run `ArtifactData list decisions` and pick the docs where `status == "queued"`. Ignore `draft` and `hold`.
2. For each one, before acting:
   - If `decision.prSha` or `prs.headSha` differs from the PR's current head on GitHub, stop for that PR. Re-review it, update its doc, set the decision back to `draft` with a note in `prs.outcome`, and tell Merill.
   - Make sure the comment still matches the fixes he ticked. If it still asks the author for a ticked fix (the fix's `ask` phrase), or says "I pushed" for a fix he left unticked, stop and ask him rather than editing his text.
3. **Fixes:** apply each ticked `fixes[].id` on the contributor's branch.
   - Use a worktree under the scratchpad, never the main checkout. The PR must have `maintainerCanModify` set.
   - Prefer merging main to rebasing, so you never force-push over a contributor's history.
   - Regenerate generated files with their build scripts, and run `./powershell/tests/pester.ps1` before pushing.
   - The commit message ends with the session's Co-Authored-By line.
   - A fix that targets main, like `builder-main`, becomes its own branch and PR off main.
4. **Review:** `event` APPROVE, REQUEST_CHANGES or COMMENT → `gh pr review <n> --approve|--request-changes|--comment --body-file <file>`. `NONE` → post nothing.
   - The comment is Merill's text, edited on the desk. Post it word for word, then add the block the page shows under "Added below your comment": a blank line, `**Changes I pushed to your branch:**`, then `- <note>` for each ticked fix that isn't `internal`, in `fixes[]` order. Leave the block out if a fix wasn't pushed, and say so in `outcome`.
   - Do the steps in the order the card's "Claude will" box lists them: internal fixes, then the branch fixes, then the review, then the merge.
   - **Assignee:** when the PR now waits on its author (REQUEST_CHANGES, or a NONE/COMMENT on a PR whose changes are still requested), assign the author: `gh pr edit <n> --add-assignee <author>`. When you approve or merge, remove the author if they are assigned: `--remove-assignee <author>`.
5. **Merge:** only if `merge` is true and CI is green on the commit you just pushed. Use `gh pr merge <n> --merge`.
   - Never enable auto-merge. If CI is still running, leave the PR and say so.
6. **Record:** update `decisions/<n>` to `status: "done"` with `doneAt`, and `prs/<n>.outcome` with one line on what happened, including links or SHAs.
   - Pin each write to the version you read, with `if_version`.
7. **Report** in chat what was posted, pushed and merged, and anything you skipped and why.

## Data schema

`prs/<number>` is written by Claude:
- **Identity:** `number`, `title`, `author`, `url`, `headSha` (12 chars), `size` (`"+a/-d · n files"`).
- **State:** `merge` (`mergeable|conflicting|behind|blocked`), `ci` (`passing|failing|pending`), `ciNote`.
- **Verdict:** `verdict` (`ready|small-fix|changes|decision|merged|closed`), `order` (rank: ready first, then by complexity).
- **Review:** `reviewedAt` (ISO), `summary`, and `question`, used only when Merill must rule on something.
- **Findings:** `findings[]`, each `{sev: high|medium|low|nit, text, where}`.
- **Fixes:** `fixes[]`, each `{id, text, note, ask, internal, preselect}`. These are things we could do ourselves.
  - `text`: what we'll do, shown beside the checkbox.
  - `note`: the line added to the comment when it's ticked, in the past tense ("Added the missing trailing newline to `x.md`.").
  - `ask`: an exact phrase from the draft comment that asks the author for the same change. The page warns when the fix is ticked and the phrase is still in the comment.
  - `internal: true` for work that isn't on the author's branch (approving fork workflows, merging main before merge). It gets no `note` and isn't mentioned in the comment.
  - Write the draft comment so it reads right with the fixes unticked. The page adds the ticked fixes' notes.
- **Draft:** `event` (`APPROVE|REQUEST_CHANGES|COMMENT|NONE`) and `comment`, which is markdown for GitHub.
- **History:** `outcome`, a one-line log of the last action.

`decisions/<number>` is written by the page:
- **Review:** `comment`, `event`, `fixes[]` (ticked ids), `merge` (bool).
- **State:** `status` (`draft|queued|hold|done`), `prSha`, `decidedAt`, and `doneAt`, which Claude sets.

Inline text renders `` `code` `` and `**bold**`.

## Writing the comment

- Address the author with their real @login, and thank them once.
- Plain English, short bullets, and bold labels for the blocking items. No emoji, and no headings beyond bold.
- Say clearly what blocks the merge and what is optional.
- When CI fails because of main, tell them it isn't their fault and that we'll fix it.
- Never write "I pushed …" in the comment. The page adds pushed fixes from their `note`, so the comment matches what is ticked.

## Process notes

Merill's rulings go here as they come up.

- Skip contributors' draft PRs.
- Read the existing reviews before reviewing.
- A benchmark test that duplicates another suite's check is a shim.
- No "(Preview)" in test titles.
- Take `headSha` from `git rev-parse --short=12` or `gh`, never typed from memory. A wrong SHA looks like a moved PR.
- A PR that merged after he queued it can't be approved. Post the comment with `gh pr comment` and record that.

skills.name: code-review
skills.content:
Review target: `2625`

`high effort → 8 inline angles → dedup (no verify) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle + 1 conventions angle, up to 6 each)

Run **8 independent finder angles** in sequence yourself, in THIS context — do NOT spawn subagents for them. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

### Conventions (CLAUDE.md)

Find the CLAUDE.md files that govern the changed code: the user-level
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the repo-root CLAUDE.md, plus any CLAUDE.md or
CLAUDE.local.md in a directory that is an ancestor of a changed file (a
directory's CLAUDE.md only applies to files at or below it). Read each one
that exists, then check the diff for clear violations of the rules they state.

Only flag a violation when you can quote the exact rule and the exact line
that breaks it — no style preferences, no vague "spirit of the doc"
inferences. In the finding, name the CLAUDE.md path and quote the rule so the
report can cite it. If no CLAUDE.md applies, return nothing for this angle.

Cleanup, altitude, and conventions candidates use the same
`file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in `failure_scenario`, state the concrete
cost (what is duplicated, wasted, harder to maintain, or which CLAUDE.md rule
is broken) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank cleanup,
altitude, and conventions findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates are the dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Dedup only (no verify)

Pool all candidates. Dedup near-duplicates only (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). Do NOT run verifiers; do NOT re-judge. Sort by severity.

## Output

Target **at least 5 findings**. If fewer genuine findings exist, emit what you have — do not invent to hit the floor.

Call the ReportFindings tool once to report this review's results
with `{level, findings}`. `findings` is at most 10 entries ranked
most-severe first; each entry has `file`, `line`, `summary`,
`short_summary` — the claim compressed to ≤60 characters, no rationale
or consequence clause — `failure_scenario`, and `category` — a short kebab-case slug for the angle
that produced it (`correctness`, `simplification`, `efficiency`,
`reuse`, `altitude`, `conventions`, or a more specific slug like
`test-coverage` when one fits better) — plus `verdict` when a verify pass
produced one. If more than 10 survive, keep the 10 most severe. If
nothing survives, call it with an empty array. Do not also print
the findings as text, and do not create or publish an artifact of the review -
the tool call is the report.


## If findings are fixed later

Whenever reported findings get fixed later in this session - the user asks you
to fix them, or later work fixes them incidentally - you MUST call ReportFindings again with the same findings, each
carrying an `outcome`: `fixed`, `no_change_needed` (the finding was wrong or
already handled), or `skipped` (real but not applied). Do not repeat the
findings as text.
Make that call immediately after the fixes land, before any prose summary; the
host UI's per-finding status updates only from it, and without it the findings
stay marked unresolved.
